and partners, we have come to realize that the concept of AI is not always easily understood  
To start this AI and Machine Learning 101 guide, we will unpack the AI puzzle by answering 
the main question many folks are asking: “What is artifcial intelligence, really?” 
The easiest way to understand artifcial intelligence is to map it to something we already 
understand—our own intelligence  How does non-artifcial, human intelligence work? At the

Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning 101
 
  
  
In machines, the input part of artifcial intelligence is exemplifed by natural language 
processing, speech recognition, visual recognition, and more  Y ou see such technologies and 
algorithms everywhere, from self-driving cars that need to sense the roadways and obstacles, 
to Alexa or Siri when it recognizes your speech  The output that follows are ways in which 
machines interact with the world around us  This might take the form of robotics, navigation 
systems (to guide those self-driving cars), speech generation (e g , Siri), etc  In between, 
we have various forms of processing that takes place  
Similar to our accrual of knowledge and memories, machines can create knowledge 
representations (e g , graph databases, ontologies) that help them store information about the 
world  Just as humans make decisions or draw inferences, machines can make a prediction, 
optimize for a target or outcome, and determine the best next steps or decisions to meet a 
specifc goal  
Finally, just as we learn by example, observation, or algorithm, machines can be taught 
using analogous methods  Supervised machine learning is much like learning by example: 
the computer is given a dataset with “labels” within the data set that act as answers, and 
eventually learns to tell the diference between diferent labels (e g , this dataset contains 
photos labeled as either “dog” or “cat”, and with enough examples, the computer will notice 
that dogs generally have longer tails and less pointy ears than cats)  
Unsupervised machine learning, on the other hand, is like learning by observation  
The computer observes patterns (dogs bark and cats meow) and, through this, learns to 
distinguish groups and patterns on its own (e g , there are two groups of animals that can be 
separated by the sound they make; one group barks—dogs—and the other group meows— 
cats)  Unsupervised learning doesn’t require labels and can therefore be preferable when data 
sets are limited and do not have labels  Finally, learning by algorithm is what happens when a 
programmer instructs a computer exactly what to do, step-by-step, in a software program  
Ideally, the most accurate and efcient artifcial intelligence results require a combination of 
learning methods  Both supervised and unsupervised machine learning are useful methods— 
it’s all about applying the right approach or approaches to the right use case  
Next, we’ll put machine learning under the microscope to understand how this part of AI 
mirrors the neurons in our brain to turn input into to optimal output

Part 3: A Brief History of Artifcial Intelligence 
For some people, the term artifcial intelligence (AI) might evoke images of futuristic cities 
with fying cars and household robots  But AI isn’t a futuristic concept, at least not anymore  
Although not referred to as such, the idea of artifcial intelligence can be traced back to 
antiquity (i e , Greek god Hephaestus’s talking mechanical handmaidens) ¹ Since the 1930s, 
scientists and mathematicians alike have been eager to explore creating true intelligence 
separate from humans  
AI’s defning moment in the mid-20th century was a happy confuence of math and biology, 
with researchers like Norbert Wiener, Claude Shannon, and Alan Turing having already chipped 
away at the intersection of electrical signals and computation  By 1943, Warren McCulloch 
and Walter Pitts had created a model for neural networks  Neural networks paved the way 
for a brave new world of computing with greater horsepower, and, in 1956, the feld of AI 
research was ofcially established as an academic discipline  
The latter half of the century was an exciting age for AI research and progress, interrupted 
occasionally by “AI winters” in the mid-70s and late 80s where AI failed to meet public 
expectations, and investment in the feld was reduced  But despite setbacks, diferent appli-
cations for AI and machine learning were appearing left and right  One particular anecdote 
of such an application has become a popular parable within the scientifc community, 
speaking quite efectively to the trials and tribulations of AI research and implementation  
The story goes something like this: 
In the 1980s, the Pentagon decided to use a neural network to identify camoufaged tanks  
Working with just one mainframe (from the 1980s, keep in mind), the neural net was trained 
with 200 pictures—100 tanks and 100 trees  Despite the relatively small neural network 
(due to 1980’s limitations on computation and memory), the lab training resulted in 100% 
accuracy  With such success, the team decides to give it a go out in the feld  The results

each  The task: analyze 10 million Y ouTube videos  The result: it found cats ² Thanks to its 
“deep learning” algorithm, the network was able to recognize cats over time, and with very 
good accuracy  
With the availability of vast computing resources that were undreamed of back in the 1980’s,

gives a system the ability to automatically “learn” through billions of combinations and 
observations, reducing the dependency on human resources  Within the cybersecurity 
domain, the method has become particularly promising for detecting malware—scenarios in 
which we have large datasets with many examples of malware from which the network 
can learn  
Unfortunately, deep learning methods are currently less efective when it comes to certain

The most common analytics we see in security today involves predictive models, which allow 
us to identify where risks might be within large amounts of data (this is where anomaly 
detection fts in)  In a nutshell, predictive modeling combines historical data with real-time 
behavior to understand or predict future behavior  With this, we can answer the question, 
“What happens next?” 
But our vision for security analytics doesn’t stop here  Predictive analytics is just one piece of 
a much larger puzzle that can give us much more useful insight for security teams  The ideal 
analytics paradigm combines intelligent sensor and ubiquitous data sources—desktops and 
servers, mobile, cloud, social networks, open data, etc —with multiple advanced analytical 
approaches to behavioral and threat analysis, including forensic analysis, risk modeling, 
anomaly detection, behavioral and response optimization, and more  
This means that we can do far more than predict or identify a threat  It allows us to go even 
further to ofer not just advanced detection but insight into how to respond most efectively  
Security analytics gives us the power to answer other key questions, like “How many threats 
are there?” and “What is the best possible reaction?” 
We haven’t seen other classes of analytics like optimization methods applied to cybersecurity 
yet, but they have immense potential  These techniques look at all the possible reactions to a 
security risk and determining the best response  Y es, there are ways to do this with math  
For example, optimization methods are used when you place a call to your cell phone service 
provider with an issue  They are not randomly making a recommendation on whether or 
not to upgrade your service plan at a discount; they rely on a set of mathematics in the 
background that looks at your call logs, the number of dropped calls, how your history 
compares with that of other users, etc  It even calculates the probability that you might 
switch to another service provider  Then, out of all the possible next steps, it computes 
the best next step to maximize customer retention  
The same math can be applied to a security team to identify a risk, provide a number of ways 
in which to react, and determine mathematically the best response to maximize containment 
of this particular risk  
The rapid rise and evolution of security threats make this type of response efciency critical  
We have more data today than ever before  Thankfully, we also have more compute power, 
better algorithms, and broader investment in research and technologies to help us make 
sense of this data through mathematics  By all accounts, we believe security analytics is 
just getting started

The most common analytics we see in security today involves predictive models, which allow 
us to identify where risks might be within large amounts of data (this is where anomaly 
detection fts in)  In a nutshell, predictive modeling combines historical data with real-time 
behavior to understand or predict future behavior  With this, we can answer the question, 
“What happens next?” 
But our vision for security analytics doesn’t stop here  Predictive analytics is just one piece of 
a much larger puzzle that can give us much more useful insight for security teams  The ideal 
analytics paradigm combines intelligent sensor and ubiquitous data sources—desktops and 
servers, mobile, cloud, social networks, open data, etc —with multiple advanced analytical 
approaches to behavioral and threat analysis, including forensic analysis, risk modeling, 
anomaly detection, behavioral and response optimization, and more  
This means that we can do far more than predict or identify a threat  It allows us to go even 
further to ofer not just advanced detection but insight into how to respond most efectively  
Security analytics gives us the power to answer other key questions, like “How many threats 
are there?” and “What is the best possible reaction?” 
We haven’t seen other classes of analytics like optimization methods applied to cybersecurity 
yet, but they have immense potential  These techniques look at all the possible reactions to a 
security risk and determining the best response  Y es, there are ways to do this with math  
For example, optimization methods are used when you place a call to your cell phone service 
provider with an issue  They are not randomly making a recommendation on whether or 
not to upgrade your service plan at a discount; they rely on a set of mathematics in the 
background that looks at your call logs, the number of dropped calls, how your history 
compares with that of other users, etc  It even calculates the probability that you might 
switch to another service provider  Then, out of all the possible next steps, it computes 
the best next step to maximize customer retention  
The same math can be applied to a security team to identify a risk, provide a number of ways 
in which to react, and determine mathematically the best response to maximize containment 
of this particular risk  
The rapid rise and evolution of security threats make this type of response efciency critical  
We have more data today than ever before  Thankfully, we also have more compute power, 
better algorithms, and broader investment in research and technologies to help us make 
sense of this data through mathematics  By all accounts, we believe security analytics is

For some people, the term artifcial intelligence (AI) might evoke images of futuristic cities

Although not referred to as such, the idea of artifcial intelligence can be traced back to

scientists and mathematicians alike have been eager to explore creating true intelligence 
separate from humans  
AI’s defning moment in the mid-20th century was a happy confuence of math and biology, 
with researchers like Norbert Wiener, Claude Shannon, and Alan Turing having already chipped

a much larger puzzle that can give us much more useful insight for security teams  The ideal 
analytics paradigm combines intelligent sensor and ubiquitous data sources—desktops and 
servers, mobile, cloud, social networks, open data, etc —with multiple advanced analytical 
approaches to behavioral and threat analysis, including forensic analysis, risk modeling, 
anomaly detection, behavioral and response optimization, and more  
This means that we can do far more than predict or identify a threat  It allows us to go even 
further to ofer not just advanced detection but insight into how to respond most efectively  
Security analytics gives us the power to answer other key questions, like “How many threats 
are there?” and “What is the best possible reaction?” 
We haven’t seen other classes of analytics like optimization methods applied to cybersecurity 
yet, but they have immense potential  These techniques look at all the possible reactions to a 
security risk and determining the best response  Y es, there are ways to do this with math  
For example, optimization methods are used when you place a call to your cell phone service 
provider with an issue  They are not randomly making a recommendation on whether or 
not to upgrade your service plan at a discount; they rely on a set of mathematics in the 
background that looks at your call logs, the number of dropped calls, how your history 
compares with that of other users, etc  It even calculates the probability that you might 
switch to another service provider  Then, out of all the possible next steps, it computes 
the best next step to maximize customer retention  
The same math can be applied to a security team to identify a risk, provide a number of ways 
in which to react, and determine mathematically the best response to maximize containment 
of this particular risk  
The rapid rise and evolution of security threats make this type of response efciency critical

Part 3: A Brief History of Artifcial Intelligence 
For some people, the term artifcial intelligence (AI) might evoke images of futuristic cities 
with fying cars and household robots  But AI isn’t a futuristic concept, at least not anymore  
Although not referred to as such, the idea of artifcial intelligence can be traced back to 
antiquity (i e , Greek god Hephaestus’s talking mechanical handmaidens) ¹ Since the 1930s, 
scientists and mathematicians alike have been eager to explore creating true intelligence 
separate from humans  
AI’s defning moment in the mid-20th century was a happy confuence of math and biology, 
with researchers like Norbert Wiener, Claude Shannon, and Alan Turing having already chipped 
away at the intersection of electrical signals and computation  By 1943, Warren McCulloch 
and Walter Pitts had created a model for neural networks  Neural networks paved the way 
for a brave new world of computing with greater horsepower, and, in 1956, the feld of AI

The most common analytics we see in security today involves predictive models, which allow 
us to identify where risks might be within large amounts of data (this is where anomaly 
detection fts in)  In a nutshell, predictive modeling combines historical data with real-time 
behavior to understand or predict future behavior  With this, we can answer the question, 
“What happens next?” 
But our vision for security analytics doesn’t stop here  Predictive analytics is just one piece of 
a much larger puzzle that can give us much more useful insight for security teams  The ideal 
analytics paradigm combines intelligent sensor and ubiquitous data sources—desktops and 
servers, mobile, cloud, social networks, open data, etc —with multiple advanced analytical 
approaches to behavioral and threat analysis, including forensic analysis, risk modeling, 
anomaly detection, behavioral and response optimization, and more  
This means that we can do far more than predict or identify a threat  It allows us to go even 
further to ofer not just advanced detection but insight into how to respond most efectively  
Security analytics gives us the power to answer other key questions, like “How many threats 
are there?” and “What is the best possible reaction?” 
We haven’t seen other classes of analytics like optimization methods applied to cybersecurity 
yet, but they have immense potential  These techniques look at all the possible reactions to a 
security risk and determining the best response  Y es, there are ways to do this with math  
For example, optimization methods are used when you place a call to your cell phone service 
provider with an issue  They are not randomly making a recommendation on whether or 
not to upgrade your service plan at a discount; they rely on a set of mathematics in the 
background that looks at your call logs, the number of dropped calls, how your history 
compares with that of other users, etc  It even calculates the probability that you might 
switch to another service provider  Then, out of all the possible next steps, it computes 
the best next step to maximize customer retention  
The same math can be applied to a security team to identify a risk, provide a number of ways 
in which to react, and determine mathematically the best response to maximize containment 
of this particular risk  
The rapid rise and evolution of security threats make this type of response efciency critical  
We have more data today than ever before  Thankfully, we also have more compute power, 
better algorithms, and broader investment in research and technologies to help us make 
sense of this data through mathematics  By all accounts, we believe security analytics is 
just getting started

1.1  Syntax Directed Definitions (SDD)
Definition — SDD: a context-free grammar where every grammar symbol is given a set of attributes, and every 
production is given a set of semantic rules that compute those attributes.
Example — SDD for E → E1 + T
Production: E → E1 + T
Semantic Rule: E.val = E1.val + T.val
Meaning: the value of the bigger expression is the sum of its two parts — exactly how a calculator evaluates 3 + 4.
1.2  Syntax Trees
Definition — Syntax Tree: a tree that shows the grammatical structure of a source string, with each interior node 
representing an operation and each leaf a variable or constant.
Example — Syntax tree for a + b * c
        +
       / \
      a   *
         / \
        b   c
The tree shows * binds tighter than +, matching normal maths rules.
1.3  S-Attributed and L-Attributed Definitions
Definition — S-Attributed Definition: an SDD that uses only synthesized attributes — values computed from 
children and passed upward. Works naturally with bottom-up (LR) parsing.
Definition — L-Attributed Definition: an SDD that allows both synthesized attributes and inherited attributes that 
depend only on parent/left-sibling values. Works with top-down parsing.
Example — Everyday analogy
S-attributed is like adding up your monthly expenses from receipts — information flows only upward (child to 
parent).
L-attributed is like a teacher passing today's date down to every student in a row, left to right — information 
flows downward and sideways too.
1.4  Type Systems
Definition — Type System: the set of rules a compiler uses to assign a type to every expression and to check that 
operations are used with compatible types.
Example — Simple type rule

Definition — Type Checking: the process of verifying that the type of an operand matches what an operator

commonly by name (name equivalence) or by structure (structural equivalence).

typedef struct {int x; int y;} Point;   struct {int x; int y;} p2;
Under name equivalence, Point and the anonymous struct are different types even though their layout is

Definition — Type Conversion (Coercion): an automatic or explicit change of a value from one type to another, 
done so an operator or assignment can proceed correctly.
Example — Implicit widening
int i = 5; float f = i;   →   compiler inserts an implicit int-to-float conversion, since this never loses information.
1.8  Intermediate Languages
Definition — Intermediate Representation (IR): a machine-independent form between the source program and 
target code — common forms are syntax trees, DAGs, postfix notation, and three address code.
Example — Postfix vs infix
Infix:  a + b * c     Postfix:  a b c * +
Postfix removes the need for parentheses and precedence rules during code generation.

Definition — Three Address Code: an intermediate code where every statement has at most one operator on the 
right side and at most three addresses (two operands, one result).
Expression: a = b * c + d * e
TAC:
  t1 = b * c

1.10  Types and Declarations
Definition — Declaration Processing: the compiler phase that records each variable's type and computes its 
storage width and offset in the symbol table as declarations are read.
Example — Offset computation
int a; float b; char c;   →   a at offset 0 (width 4), b at offset 4 (width 4), c at offset 8 (width 1).
1.11  Translation of Expressions
Definition — Expression Translation: the systematic generation of three address code for an expression by 
translating each subtree of its syntax tree and combining the results.
Example — Translating a + b * c
t1 = b * c
t2 = a + t1
The multiplication is translated first because * has higher precedence and appears deeper in the syntax tree.

Definition — Back Patching: a technique for generating code for boolean expressions and control statements in a 
single pass by leaving the target of a jump instruction incomplete and filling it in later once the target address is 
known.
Example — Why it's needed
For if (a < b) goto L, the compiler often doesn't know the actual instruction number for L yet — so it leaves a blank 
and patches it in once that label's address is fixed.

  PART 2 — ELABORATE NOTES.
2.1  Syntax Directed Definitions (SDD)
A Syntax Directed Definition attaches attributes to grammar symbols and semantic rules to productions. Every 
time a production is used during parsing, its semantic rule tells the compiler how to compute some value — like 
the numeric result of an expression, the type of a variable, or the generated code.
Attributes are of two kinds:
• Synthesized attribute — computed from the attribute values of the children of a node (flows bottom-up).
• Inherited attribute — computed from the attribute values of the parent and/or siblings (flows top-down or 
left-to-right).
Production Semantic Rule Meaning
E → E1 + T E.val = E1.val + T.val add the two sub-values
E → T E.val = T.val copy value upward
T → T1 * F T.val = T1.val * F.val multiply the two sub-values
F → ( E ) F.val = E.val value of parenthesised expr
F → id F.val = id.lexval look up the identifier's value
Example — Real-time example — a billing calculator
Think of a shop billing app evaluating quantity * price + tax. Each time the app combines two numbers, it is 
silently applying a semantic rule identical to E.val = E1.val + T.val.
This is exactly the mechanism compilers use to evaluate constant expressions during compilation (constant 
folding).
2.2  Syntax Trees and DAGs
A syntax tree represents the essential structure of a program in a more compact form than a parse tree — 
operators become interior nodes and operands become leaves, with no nodes for chain productions like E → T 
→ F.
A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) goes one step further: if the same sub-expression appears more than once, the 
DAG reuses a single node instead of duplicating it, exposing common sub-expressions.
Example — Syntax tree vs DAG for a + a * (b - c) + (b - c) * d
The sub-expression (b - c) appears twice.
A syntax tree draws two separate (b - c) subtrees.
A DAG draws (b - c) only once and lets both '*' operations point to that single node — this is the theoretical basis 
for common sub-expression elimination, a real optimisation used in GCC and every industrial compiler.
2.3  S-Attributed and L-Attributed Definitions

Key concepts include constant folding, attribute flow (bottom‑up for synthesized, top‑down/left‑to‑right for inherited), and the distinction between S‑Attributed and L‑Attributed definitions.

S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes. Because values only ever flow upward from children to 
parent, they can be evaluated naturally during a bottom-up (LR) parse, simply by computing each attribute when 
its production is reduced.
L-attributed definitions allow inherited attributes too, but only in a restricted, left-to-right way: an inherited 
attribute of a symbol on the right side of a production may depend only on attributes of the production's left 
side, or on attributes of symbols to its left. This restriction is exactly what makes L-attributed definitions safe to 
evaluate during a single left-to-right depth-first parse (used in top-down / recursive-descent parsing).
How to identify which kind an SDD is
Look at every semantic rule for inherited attributes referencing anything to the right — if none exist, and only 
children feed the parent, it's S-attributed.
If inherited attributes exist but only ever look left or up, it's L-attributed. If an inherited attribute needs a value 
from the right, it is neither, and needs multiple parsing passes or attribute grammars with global rules.
Example — Real-time example — a form validator
A web form that passes today's date down into every 'age' field (inherited, parent → children) and then collects 
validation results back up to show one summary error box (synthesized, children → parent) is behaving like an L-
attributed definition.
2.4  Type Systems
A type system is a set of rules that assigns a type to every expression in a program and defines which operations 
are legal between which types. Its two jobs are: preventing meaningless operations (like adding a string to a 
boolean) and enabling the compiler to choose the correct machine instructions and storage layout for each 
value.
Type systems are classified as:
• Static typing — types are checked at compile time (C, Java, our CS4501 running examples).
• Dynamic typing — types are checked at run time (Python, JavaScript).
• Strong typing — no silent, unsafe conversions are allowed; Weak typing — many implicit conversions are 
allowed.
Example — Real-time example
When you write int total = quantity * price; in C, the compiler's type system decides at compile time that quantity 
and price (both int) multiply to give an int — no runtime check is needed, which is why compiled C code runs 
faster than an equivalent Python script.
2.5  Type Checking
A type checker verifies that the type of each operand matches what the corresponding operator expects, using 
type rules built into the compiler's semantic analysis phase. It works over the same syntax-directed framework 
as Section 2.1 — every expression gets a 'type' attribute in addition to its 'val' attribute.
Rule Pattern Type Rule
E → E1 + E2 if E1.type = E2.type = int then E.type = int; if either is float 
then E.type = float
E → E1 and E2 if E1.type = E2.type = bool then E.type = bool, else type-
error

Two types are equivalent if the compiler treats them as interchangeable. There are two common definitions:
• Name equivalence — two types are the same only if they share the same declared name.
• Structural equivalence — two types are the same if they have the same structure (same fields, in the same 
order, with the same types), regardless of name.
Example — Real-time example
typedef int Meters; typedef int Feet;
Under name equivalence, a Meters value cannot be assigned directly to a Feet variable even though both are 
really int — this is exactly how languages like Ada prevent unit-mixing bugs (e.g. the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter 
loss, caused by mixing metric and imperial units).
2.7  Type Conversions (Coercion)
When an operator or assignment involves mismatched types, the compiler inserts a conversion. Conversions are 
either:
• Implicit (coercion) — inserted automatically by the compiler, usually only in the 'widening' direction (int → 
float) so no data is lost.
• Explicit (casting) — written by the programmer, e.g. (int) 3.99, which may lose information (narrowing).

int i = 5; float f = i; implicit widening int→float f = 5.0
float g = 5.9; int k = (int) g; explicit narrowing float→int k = 5 (fraction truncated)

float total = 19.99 * 3;  printed as 59.97000123 due to floating point widening — a real reason financial software 
uses fixed-point/decimal types instead of float, to avoid conversion precision loss.
2.8  Intermediate Languages
An intermediate representation (IR) sits between the source program and the target machine code. It lets a 
compiler support many source languages and many target machines without writing a separate front end/back 
end for every combination (this is exactly the design GCC and LLVM use).

2.9  Three Address Code (TAC)
Three Address Code is the most widely used intermediate representation. Every TAC statement has the general 
form x = y op z, where op is a single operator and there are at most three addresses (two operands and a result). 
Complex expressions are broken into a sequence of such statements using compiler-generated temporary 
variables (t1, t2, ...).

2.10  Types and Declarations
When the compiler processes a declaration, it must record in the symbol table: the variable's type, its width 
(bytes needed), and its offset (position relative to the start of its storage area, such as an activation record). This 
groundwork is essential before any code generation can happen, because every later TAC instruction that reads 
or writes a variable needs to know exactly where it lives.
A running 'offset' counter is maintained as declarations are processed left to right; each new variable is placed at 
the current offset, and the offset is then advanced by that variable's width.

2.12  Back Patching
For boolean expressions and control-flow statements (if, while, for), the target label of a jump instruction is 
often not known at the moment the jump instruction itself is generated — the label might belong to code that 
appears later. Back patching solves this in a single compiler pass:
• Generate the jump instruction, but leave its target field blank.
• Add the instruction's own position to a list associated with the appropriate attribute (truelist, falselist, or 
nextlist).
• Once the real target address becomes known (e.g. we reach the code for the 'then' branch), patch every 
instruction in the list with that address.
Two key functions used throughout: makelist(i) creates a new list containing only instruction i; merge(p1, p2) 
concatenates two lists; backpatch(list, addr) fills in addr as the target for every instruction in list.

2.13  Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) Schemes and Predictive Translators
An SDD specifies WHAT a translation computes, but deliberately leaves open WHEN each semantic rule fires 
during parsing. A Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) scheme is the implementation-ready counterpart: it embeds 
semantic actions directly inside the production body at the exact point they should execute, fixing the 
evaluation order. This is the notation actually used to build a working translator.
Definition — Predictive Translator: a top-down, table-driven translator that selects the correct production for a 
non-terminal using only that non-terminal and one token of lookahead (no backtracking), firing embedded 
semantic actions as it goes so the translation is produced as a side effect of parsing.
Because a predictive parser commits to a production the moment it sees the lookahead token, its actions must 
fire in a strictly pinned-down order -- which is precisely what an SDT (not a plain SDD) provides. Building one 
requires an LL(1) parsing table, constructed in five steps:
• Step 1: Eliminate left recursion (A -> Aa | b becomes A -> bA', A' -> aA' | eps) and left-factor productions 
sharing a common prefix.
• Step 2: Compute FIRST for every non-terminal, then FOLLOW for every non-terminal (starting with $ in 
FOLLOW of the start symbol).
• Step 3: Build table M[A,a]: place A->alpha in M[A,a] for every a in FIRST(alpha); if eps is in FIRST(alpha), also 
place it in M[A,b] for every b in FOLLOW(A).
• Step 4: To parse, trace a stack starting with $ and the start symbol: pop a non-terminal and push 
M[top,token]'s right side (reversed); pop and match a terminal directly against the input. Stop when both 
stack and input show only $.
• Step 5 (error handling): a blank table cell signals a syntax error; if the current token is in FOLLOW(A), panic-
mode recovery simply pops A and continues, treating it as if A had matched empty input.
FIRST and FOLLOW rules (memorise these)
FIRST(X): if X is a terminal, FIRST(X)={X}. If X->eps, add eps. If X->Y1Y2...Yk, add FIRST(Y1)-{eps}, and continue 
adding FIRST(Yi) for each further Yi only while every earlier Yj can derive eps; add eps itself only if ALL Yi can 
derive eps.
FOLLOW(A): $ is in FOLLOW(start symbol). For A->aBb, add FIRST(b)-{eps} to FOLLOW(B). For A->aB, or if eps is in 
FIRST(b), add all of FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B) as well.
Example — Worked LL(1) table and trace for E->TE'|.., translating id+id*id
Table (rows E,E',T,T',F; columns id,+,*,(,),$) is built from FIRST/FOLLOW exactly as in Section 2.13 Step 3.
Tracing the stack against id+id*id produces the parse E->TE', T->FT', F->id, T'->eps, E'->+TE', T->FT', F->id, T'->*FT', 
F->id, T'->eps, E'->eps.
If a print action fires right after each token is matched or each production completes, the emitted order is id id id 
* + -- the correct postfix form, confirming precedence is respected purely by parse order.
2.14  Dependency Graphs and Attribute Evaluation Order
Once an SDD mixes synthesized and inherited attributes freely, it is no longer obvious that a simple bottom-up 
or top-down pass will compute every attribute before it is needed. A dependency graph makes this explicit: for 
every attribute instance at every parse-tree node, draw an edge M -> N whenever attribute N's semantic rule 
reads attribute M's value. A valid evaluation order is then any topological sort of this graph -- an order in which 
every node appears after all the nodes with edges pointing into it.

Section 2.4 introduced type systems informally; this section adds the formal notation compilers use internally to 
represent a type, plus the distinction between when a type is actually checked.
Definition — Type Expression: a formal notation for a type, built either from a basic type (integer, real, char, 
boolean, void) or by applying a type constructor -- array(n,T), pointer(T), T1 x T2 (product/record), or T1 -> T2 
(function) -- to smaller type expressions.
Checking Style When It Happens Trade-off
Static typing Compile time, before the program 
runs
Catches errors early, no runtime cost, 
but less flexible
Dynamic typing Run time, as each operation executes More flexible (e.g. duck typing), but 
adds runtime overhead and errors 
surface later
How to solve a type-checking problem step by step
Step 1: draw (or imagine) the expression tree; note the declared type of every leaf (variable/literal).
Step 2: work bottom-up -- at every operator node, look up both children's already-computed types.
Step 3: apply the type rule table to decide this node's result type, inserting a conversion instruction into the TAC 
if a type had to be widened.
Step 4: if no rule matches, assign type_error to this node and let it propagate upward as the node's type -- do not 
keep re-deriving further mismatches from an already-errored subtree.
Step 5: the type at the ROOT is the type of the whole expression.

P.1  Problem 1 — Construct an SDD and evaluate it for 3 * 4 + 5
Step 1 — Identify the grammar and attribute. We use E→E+T | T, T→T*F | F, F→(E) | digit, with one synthesized 
attribute val on every non-terminal, meaning 'the numeric value this subtree represents.'
Step 2 — Parse the input bottom-up. Because * has higher precedence than +, the grammar's structure forces 3 
* 4 to be reduced first (it becomes a single T), and only afterwards is + applied at the E level. This is precisely 
why this grammar family (with separate E and T levels) enforces correct precedence without needing explicit 
precedence rules.
Step 3 — Apply the semantic rule at every reduction, in the exact order the parser reduces:
Parse: (3 * 4) + 5
F -> 3        F.val = 3
F -> 4        F.val = 4
T -> T * F    T.val = 3 * 4 = 12
F -> 5        F.val = 5
T -> F        T.val = 5
E -> E + T    E.val = 12 + 5 = 17
Final Answer: E.val = 17
Step 4 — Interpret the result. Notice that val is synthesized purely bottom-up: each rule only reads the val of its 
own children, never anything from outside the subtree. This is exactly the S-attributed pattern from Section 1.3 / 
2.3, which is why this SDD can be evaluated directly during an LR parse with no extra passes.
Common mistake to avoid
Students often apply E -> E + T before T -> T * F is fully reduced. Always finish reducing the higher-precedence 
subtree (T, from *) completely before combining it at the E level -- this mirrors the actual bottom-up parse order, 
not the left-to-right reading order of the expression.

P.8  Problem 8 — Translate while (a < b) do a = a + 1 using backpatching
Step 1 — Unlike if, a while loop must return to re-test its condition after every iteration, so the very first step is 
to save the instruction number where the condition test begins -- call it the begin label.
Step 2 — Generate the conditional jump for the test (truelist) and the jump for loop exit (falselist), exactly as in 
Problem 7.
Step 3 — Once we reach the first instruction of the loop body, backpatch truelist to that address.
Step 4 — After the loop body's last instruction, generate an unconditional jump back to the saved begin label -- 
this is what actually forms the loop.
Step 5 — Once we reach the first instruction after the whole while statement, backpatch falselist to that 
address.
100: if a < b goto 102       (begin label = 100, E.truelist={100})
101: goto _                  (E.falselist={101}, will exit loop)
102: t1 = a + 1
103: a = t1
104: goto 100                <- unconditional jump BACK to re-test condition
105: <code after while>      <- backpatch(E.falselist, 105): instr 101 -> 'goto 105'
Why while needs a saved 'begin' label but if doesn't
A while loop must jump back to re-check its condition every iteration, so the compiler must remember the 
instruction number where the condition test starts (100 here) -- this is the one detail students most often forget 
in exams.
P.9  Problem 9 — Generate TAC for the assignment statement a[i] = b[j] + c
Step 1 — Recognise that array references need an address computation before the value can be read or written 
-- a[i] means 'go to the memory address of a, offset by i times the element width.'
Step 2 — Translate the right-hand side first: read b[j] using an indexed load, add c, and store the result in a 
temporary.
Step 3 — Translate the left-hand side as an indexed store, writing the temporary into a[i].
t1 = j * 4          (assume int elements, width 4 -- compute byte offset for b[j])
t2 = b[t1]          (indexed load: read b[j])
t3 = t2 + c

P.10  Problem 10 — Translate the boolean expression a < b and c < d using 
backpatching
Step 1 — Recall the short-circuit rule for 'and': if the first operand is false, the whole expression is false 
immediately, and the second operand should not even be evaluated.
Step 2 — Translate the first comparison a < b. If it's true, control must fall through to test the second 
comparison -- so its truelist is not patched yet, it simply continues to the next instruction. If it's false, the whole 
expression is false, so its falselist becomes part of the overall expression's falselist directly.
Step 3 — Translate the second comparison c < d. Its truelist and falselist become the truelist and falselist of the 
entire 'and' expression.
100: if a < b goto 102        (fall through on true -- no jump needed, so control just 
continues)
101: goto _                   (falselist of a<b joins the falselist of the whole 
expression)
102: if c < d goto _          (this becomes the truelist of the whole expression)
103: goto _                   (this joins the falselist of the whole expression)
Overall: truelist = {102}, falselist = {101, 103}
Key idea examiners test here
The defining feature of 'and' translation is that the first operand's TRUE case does NOT jump anywhere -- it just 
falls through into the code for the second operand. Only the FALSE case of the first operand needs an explicit 
jump (to skip evaluating the second operand entirely) -- this is what implements short-circuit evaluation.
P.11  Problem 11 — Construct the syntax-directed translation scheme for a 
procedure call p(a, b+c)
Step 1 — Recall that each actual parameter of a procedure call must be evaluated to a temporary (or simple 
address) before the call itself is issued, since a call statement can only reference simple addresses, not full sub-
expressions.
Step 2 — Translate each parameter expression left to right, generating a param statement immediately after 
each one is ready.
Step 3 — Once all parameters are queued, generate the call statement, naming the procedure and the 
parameter count n.
param a          (first actual parameter is simple, no computation needed)
t1 = b + c
param t1         (second actual parameter, computed first)
call p, 2        (n = 2 actual parameters)
Step 4 — Note that the parameter count n in call p, n is essential for the callee to know how much stack space 
the caller has pushed -- omitting it is a very common mark-losing mistake.

P.13  Problem 13 — Translate the 2D array assignment A[i,j] := B[i,j] + C[k]
Step 1 — Recall the row-major address formula for a 2D array A with dimensions n1 x n2, lower bounds low1, 
low2, and element width w: address(A[i,j]) = ((i - low1) * n2 + (j - low2)) * w + base_A. This simplifies to one per-
array constant (folding in base_A and the lower bounds) plus a per-access offset that depends only on i and j.
Step 2 — Assume A, B are 10x20 int arrays (n2=20, w=4, low1=low2=1) and C has 50 elements. The constant for 
A and B becomes c = base_A - (1*20+1)*4 = base_A - 84 (and similarly for B).

t2 := c1          t7 := 4*k           (c1 = base_A - 84)
t3 := 4*t1        t8 := c3            (c3 = base_C, since C is 1-D)

(column offset), one more multiply (by element width w), and one indexed load/store -- four operations 
regardless of how large the array is, because the per-array constant is computed once and reused.

101: x   := t1
102: t2 := addr_of x     (address-of: t2 gets the address of x)

  PART 4 — PART A (2 MARK) QUESTION BANK
Q1. What is a Syntax Directed Definition (SDD)?
Ans: An SDD is a context-free grammar in which every grammar symbol carries a set of attributes, and every 
production has an associated semantic rule defining how those attributes are computed. It specifies WHAT a 
translation computes without fixing WHEN each rule fires -- e.g. E->E1+T with rule E.val=E1.val+T.val.
Q2. Differentiate an SDD from a Syntax Directed Translation (SDT) scheme.
Ans: An SDD leaves the evaluation order of its semantic rules unspecified. An SDT embeds semantic actions 
directly inside the production body at the exact point they must execute, fixing that order -- which is what a 
predictive (top-down) translator needs, since it commits to actions as it parses left to right.
Q3. Differentiate synthesized and inherited attributes.
Ans: A synthesized attribute's value at a node is computed from its CHILDREN, so information flows bottom-up 
(e.g. E.val=E1.val+T.val). An inherited attribute's value comes from its PARENT or LEFT SIBLINGS, so information 
flows top-down or left-to-right (e.g. passing a declared type down to every identifier in a list).
Q4. What is an annotated parse tree?
Ans: A parse tree in which every node is labelled with the value of its computed attribute(s) -- for example, 
showing E.val=17 written directly at the E node after evaluating 3*4+5.
Q5. What is a dependency graph, and how is it used?
Ans: A graph with one edge M->N for every attribute instance N whose semantic rule reads attribute M's value. 
A valid evaluation order is any topological sort of this graph; for a purely S-attributed SDD every edge points 
child-to-parent, so post-order traversal alone is already a valid order.
Q6. What is a syntax tree?
Ans: A compact tree representing a program's grammatical structure, with operators/keywords as interior nodes 
and operands as leaves; nodes for symbols with no semantic meaning (like parentheses, or chain productions 
such as E->T->F) are omitted.
Q7. How does a DAG differ from a syntax tree?
Ans: A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is built the same way as a syntax tree, but before creating a new node it 
checks whether an identical node (same operator, same children) already exists -- if so it reuses that node 
instead of duplicating it, exposing repeated sub-expressions for optimisation.
Q8. Define S-attributed definition.
Ans: An SDD in which every attribute is synthesized. Because values only ever flow upward from children to 
parent, an S-attributed SDD can always be evaluated during a single bottom-up (LR) parse, with no extra passes 
needed.
Q9. Define L-attributed definition.
Ans: An SDD that also allows inherited attributes, but only under the restriction that an inherited attribute may 
depend solely on the parent's attributes or on attributes of symbols strictly to its LEFT in the same production -- 
this restriction is what keeps it evaluable in one left-to-right, depth-first (top-down) pass.
Q10. What is a predictive translator, and what grammar property does it require?
